docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
On your laptop, in five minutes: a miss, a reuse, a changed input and a rejected result.

You need aval (Install), Docker and openssl. Run the blocks in order in one shell. Each text block is the expected output; ... is a digest that changes on every run.

docs.title: 1. Set up
docs.text:
A local OCI registry (port 5001: macOS uses 5000 for AirPlay):

docker run -d --name aval-registry -p 5001:5000 registry:2

A project: one input file and aval.yaml, which names the test command and the files it reads (scope):

mkdir aval-demo && cd aval-demo
mkdir src && echo hello > src/hello.txt
cat > aval.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: hello
runner:
  command: ["grep", "-q", "hello", "src/hello.txt"]
scope:
  source: ["src/**"]
cacheability: hermetic
EOF

A signing key (ECDSA P-256) and a policy that trusts it:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key
openssl pkey -in aval.key -pubout -out aval.pub
cat > policy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: developer
identities:
  - publicKey: aval.pub
    trustLevel: developer
EOF

docs.title: 2. First run: a miss
docs.text:
This run has no --policy, so Aval does not look for a result. It runs the test, then --push signs the result with aval.key and pushes it:

aval run --push --key aval.key --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval

test hello fingerprint sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
miss hello sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
reason: no trust policy configured: pass --policy to reuse verified results
ran hello: passed (exit 0)
pushed localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...

docs.title: 3. Second run: a reuse
docs.text:
Check that a result you trust exists for these exact inputs:

aval verify --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml
echo "exit code: $?"

verified hello sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
signer: key ..., trust level developer
reference: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
exit code: 0

Run again. Aval finds the trusted result and skips the test:

aval run --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml

test hello fingerprint sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
verified hello sha256:fb3906f246f9255cf129e24de1256ac47b85e33cc548f3f517e94e237db0de06
signer: key ..., trust level developer
reference: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
reused passed result

docs.title: 4. Change an input: a miss again
docs.text:
Edit a file in scope. The fingerprint changes, so nothing matches and the test runs:

echo "hello, world" > src/hello.txt
aval run --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml

test hello fingerprint sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
miss hello sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
reason: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval: no attestation found for fingerprint
ran hello: passed (exit 0)

docs.title: 5. A result from an untrusted signer: exit 5
docs.text:
Someone who can push to the registry, but with a key your policy does not trust, publishes a result. Aval rejects it, runs the test and exits 5: a security event, not a miss. A tampered result ends the same way:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out other.key
aval run --push --key other.key --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval
aval run --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval --policy policy.yaml
echo "exit code: $?"

test hello fingerprint sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
miss hello sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
reason: no trust policy configured: pass --policy to reuse verified results
ran hello: passed (exit 0)
pushed localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
test hello fingerprint sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
aval: SECURITY: 1 attestation(s) for hello failed signature or policy verification; treat it as a security event, see https://github.com/TrianaLab/aval/blob/main/docs/trust-model.md
verification-failed hello sha256:d52167b48089d3c3add62a6e81c6bfb0aa8d90baa98a69235c48bd892297170b
reference: localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval@sha256:...
reason: attestation verification failed: signature: signer key id "..." is not in the trust policy (trust policy policy.yaml)
ran hello: passed (exit 0)
exit code: 5

docs.title: What just happened
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  files[src/hello.txt<br>listed in scope] --> fp[fingerprint<br>sha256:fb39...]
  fp --> look{result for this<br>fingerprint?}
  look -- no --> miss([miss: run the test<br>steps 2 and 4]):::muted
  look -- "yes, signer in policy.yaml" --> ok([verified: reuse,<br>skip the test<br>step 3]):::ok
  look -- "yes, only untrusted signers" --> bad([verification-failed:<br>run the test, exit 5<br>step 5]):::err

The fingerprint covers only what scope lists. See Outcomes and Trust.

Stop the registry when you are done:

docker rm -f aval-registry

Next: write a contract for your own test, then use GitHub Actions and sign results without a key.

docs.title: Stats
docs.text:
Live reuse numbers from every repository that records its runs to TrianaLab's public stats registry, ghcr.io/trianalab/aval-stats. Aval's own CI is one of them.

Live statistics are not available right now: stats.json is missing, malformed or more than 6 hours old.

Run records are unsigned statistics. They never affect reuse.

docs.title: Where the numbers come from
docs.text:
Twice an hour, and on every push to main, the docs workflow reads the registry anonymously:

aval stats --registry ghcr.io/trianalab/aval-stats \
  --by repository --since 30d -o json

It publishes the stats report, plus generatedAt, as stats.json at the root of this site. This page and the home page read that file in your browser. If a refresh fails, the previous file stays.

To keep statistics for your own repositories, see Measure reuse. To add a TrianaLab repository to these numbers, see CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Trust model
docs.text: Formats are frozen; see artifact format.

docs.title: What a signature proves
docs.text:
An attestation is a DSSE envelope around an in-toto Statement whose predicate says: "test test.id, with inputs hashing to execution.fingerprint, produced result on subject".

Proves Does not prove who signed: an OIDC issuer and subject (keyless), or a key that the test ran that nobody changed the claim since that it ran honestly (unmodified test code, no skipped cases, no patched runner) that inputs not declared in aval.yaml were the same

Reuse needs all three: a valid signature, a signer the policy trusts at a high enough level, and a fingerprint and test id that match what Aval computed locally. The predicate's runner block is only a claim: identity comes from the verified signer, level from the policy. A key signer matches only publicKey entries, a keyless signer only issuer + subjectRegexp entries.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
Mode Where Signs with Rekor Usual level keyless CI an ephemeral key and a short-lived Fulcio certificate for the OIDC token in $SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN always (the certificate expires in minutes; Rekor's timestamp keeps it verifiable) runner key local an unencrypted ECDSA P-256 PEM key (PKCS#8 or SEC1); Cosign keys are encrypted and not supported no developer

Make a key with openssl ecparam -name prime256v1 -genkey -noout -out aval.key. Getting the OIDC token is the caller's job, so no CI vendor or issuer is assumed.

Signing always uses the Sigstore public-good instance (https://fulcio.sigstore.dev, https://rekor.sigstore.dev) (TODO(milestone-5): signing against a private Sigstore deployment; verification already accepts its pinned trustedRoot).

docs.title: Trust levels
docs.text:
Higher is stronger:

Level Name Constant Who Good for 0 unknown TrustUnknown level could not be established never accepted 1 developer TrustDeveloper a developer's local signature personal acceleration only: skip a test you already ran on your machine. Not full trust. 2 runner TrustRunner a CI runner with a verifiable workload identity (e.g. GitHub Actions OIDC) reuse in CI. CI should require at least this level. 3 isolated TrustIsolated an isolated execution with a verifiable attestation of the environment itself reuse where the runner host is not trusted either

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: The trust policy decides which signers are accepted and at what level.

docs.title: Policy file
docs.text:
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner           # developer | runner | isolated
# trustedRoot: sigstore/trusted_root.json  # keyless only; default: Sigstore public-good, fetched with TUF
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/acme/orders/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner
  - publicKey: keys/alice.pub   # PEM public key file
    trustLevel: developer
allowedCacheability: [external-dependencies]
Field Meaning identities the signers you accept: each is an OIDC issuer plus a subjectRegexp matched against the whole certificate subject, or a publicKey PEM file. At least one. trustLevel the level an identity gets: developer, runner or isolated. minTrustLevel the lowest level a result needs to be reused. allowedCacheability classes reused besides hermetic and controlled-environment; only external-dependencies has an effect, and non-deterministic is rejected. trustedRoot a pinned Sigstore trusted root for keyless signatures; without it, the public-good root is fetched.

Relative publicKey and trustedRoot paths are read from the policy file's directory. A policy with an unknown field, a bad level or identity, or more than one document is rejected, never half-read (every policy error).

docs.title: Verification order
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  sig{signature valid?} -- yes --> who{signer in<br>the policy?}
  who -- yes --> st{statement and predicate<br>well-formed, subject matches?}
  st -- yes --> fp{fingerprint and<br>test id match?}
  fp -- yes --> cls{signed cacheability equals<br>the contract's?}
  cls -- yes --> lvl{level ≥<br>minTrustLevel?}
  lvl -- yes --> ok([verified]):::ok
  lvl -- no --> miss([miss, exit 4]):::muted
  sig -- no --> bad([verification-failed, exit 5]):::err
  who -- no --> bad
  st -- no --> bad
  fp -- no --> bad
  cls -- no --> bad

A class the policy does not allow (non-deterministic, or external-dependencies not in allowedCacheability) is a miss before any lookup.

A result whose only problem is a level below minTrustLevel, such as a developer result under a CI policy, is routine non-reuse: a miss, listed in rejected, never a security event. Go callers of evidence.Verify get ErrVerification for a level below the minimum; the CLI treats it as a miss.

Signature checks (sigstore-go, against the bundle stored next to the envelope):

  • Keyless: chains to a Fulcio CA in the trusted root, has an embedded SCT from a trusted CT log, a Rekor entry, and a trusted timestamp inside the certificate's validity.
  • Key: verifies with one of the policy's public keys; no Rekor entry.
  • Both: the envelope must be the exact one the bundle signs; no bundle means no verification.

Without --policy nothing is trusted and nothing is looked up: miss. A policy or trusted root that cannot load: outcome error (exit 1), and the test runs.

docs.title: Keyless verification needs the network and a writable HOME
docs.text:
Keyless policies without trustedRoot fetch the Sigstore root with TUF (tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev) the first time a candidate carries a certificate, and cache it in $HOME/.sigstore. Offline or with a read-only HOME, that candidate is error (never verification-failed) and the test runs. A miss or a key-based result never fetches it.

To avoid the dependency, pin the trusted root in the policy:

  1. Get trusted_root.json once, on a machine with network access. After one keyless aval verify there, sigstore-go has it at $HOME/.sigstore/root/tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev/targets/trusted_root.json.
  2. Commit it next to the policy and set trustedRoot: trusted_root.json (relative to the policy file).
  3. Refresh it when Sigstore rotates keys: a stale root fails to verify new certificates (outcome verification-failed), so watch for that after a Sigstore announcement.

Policies with only publicKey identities never fetch anything.

docs.title: Fail closed
docs.text:
If Aval cannot prove that a previous execution is equivalent and trusted, the test runs.

  • Fingerprint errors (empty scope, a glob that matches nothing, a symlink, an unreadable file): nothing to look up; the test runs.
  • Registry errors (unreachable, auth): outcome error, exit 1; the test runs.
  • Malformed manifest or moved tag: verification failure, exit 5.
  • Consume by digest: the tag sha256-<fingerprint hex> is only an index; everything after lookup uses repo@sha256:... (lookup).
  • No silent replacement: pushes only add results. Every candidate is verified and the highest trusted level wins. A candidate that fails verification is listed in rejected and stays visible; one that cannot be fetched or checked blocks reuse.
  • Unknown or missing fields in aval.yaml: rejected, exit 2.

aval run --no-reuse always runs and never looks anything up. What each outcome does: Outcomes.

docs.title: Safeguards in aval run
docs.text:
• $SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN is removed from the environment before runner.command starts, so the code under test cannot sign as the CI job.
  • A --report that cannot be written disables reuse: the test runs, and a verification failure still exits 5.
  • Reasons from attestations are escaped on text output and stderr (\n, \x1b, \u2028), so they never start a line of their own; the JSON report keeps them as is.
  • --shadow verifies and runs the test anyway, and exits 1 with aval: FALSE HIT: ... when a verified result disagrees with the real run.
  • --record publishes an unsigned run record for every outcome; it never affects reuse or the exit code (run records).

docs.title: Miss vs verification failure
docs.text:
Outcome Go error verified nil miss wraps evidence.ErrNotFound (a level below minTrustLevel: CLI only) verification-failed wraps evidence.ErrVerification; *evidence.VerificationError carries the reason error any other

A verification failure means someone published a result under this fingerprint that does not verify. Run the test and surface it: fail the job or alert. Never fold it into a silent re-run.

docs.title: Cacheability classes
docs.text:
The class is part of the contract, so it is part of the fingerprint, and it is copied into the predicate as test.cacheability.

Class Use it when Reused hermetic the test reads only the declared files yes controlled-environment it uses services you pin, such as a Compose image by digest yes external-dependencies it calls something you do not control only if the policy allows it non-deterministic the same inputs can give a different result never

A candidate whose signed test.cacheability differs from the local contract's is a verification failure.

docs.title: Threats
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Compromised developer key Policy grants developer identities level 1 at most; CI sets minTrustLevel >= 2, so a stolen developer key cannot satisfy CI. It can still poison that developer's own reuse. Prefer keyless (short-lived Fulcio certs, Rekor log) over long-lived keys. Tag swapping (sha256-<fp> repointed to another manifest) Tag is lookup only and must resolve to the fingerprint's deterministic anchor manifest; any other target is verification-failed. Candidates are the anchor's referrers, fetched and verified by digest. Replay of a passing result for a different fingerprint or test id Verification requires the signed fingerprint and test id to equal the ones computed locally. The signed predicate cannot be re-labeled without breaking the signature. Mismatch is verification-failed. Undeclared input changed (file outside scope, unlisted env var, network service) Not detected: the fingerprint only covers declared inputs. Mitigated by contract review, external-dependencies not being reusable by default and non-deterministic never being reusable, and the false-hit suite. Observed-input tracing is future work. Content behind a declared name changed (repushed image tag, new upstream release, changed remote script) The scanner reports the mutable references it recognizes in the scope and runner.command; for hermetic and controlled-environment an unaccepted one makes the lookup a miss and blocks publishing. Accepting one needs scope.allowMutable, which changes the fingerprint and shows in review. References it does not recognize stay a known gap (Pin your dependencies). Registry compromise (attacker can write arbitrary manifests and tags) Cannot forge signatures, so it cannot produce reuse on its own; injected attestations show up as verification-failed, or, when another candidate verifies, as a rejected entry with an aval: SECURITY: ... line on stderr. It can delete attestations (forcing re-runs) or deny service (error, re-run). Availability is out of scope. Forged or tampered run records (anyone with push access) Unsigned statistics, never read by aval run or aval verify; aval stats skips malformed records and caps how many it reads. Dishonest but trusted signer (ran a modified test and signed "passed") Out of scope for Aval. A signature proves who claims it, not that the test ran honestly. Limit which identities get which level; level 3 (isolated) exists for this.

docs.title: Thesis
docs.text:
Aval turns test results into signed, verifiable OCI artifacts. An expensive test runs once, locally or in CI. The result is published to an OCI registry as a signed attestation bound to a deterministic fingerprint of the test's inputs. Any other environment computes the same fingerprint, finds the attestation, verifies it, and if the trust policy allows it, reuses the result instead of running the test again.

This is not a test cache. A cache optimizes for hit rate and quietly tolerates a stale entry now and then. Aval optimizes for being able to justify every reuse, and when it can't, it runs the test.

A signature proves who claims the test passed, not that it ran honestly or against the inputs you have now. So reuse needs an explicit input contract (aval.yaml), so "same inputs" can be checked, and a trust policy over signer identities, so "who ran it" can be accepted or rejected.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text: Heavy tests (integration, end-to-end, hardware, long suites) re-run on every pipeline, branch and environment even when nothing they depend on changed. Teams pay for it in time and compute, or skip tests on informal judgment that nobody can audit. Build caches solve this only for teams on a hermetic build system.

docs.title: Design decisions
docs.text: Decision Why No own infrastructure: ORAS, Sigstore (sigstore-go), in-toto/DSSE, OCI 1.1 referrers. Lookup by the tag sha256-<fingerprint hex>, consumption by digest registries, signing and access control already exist and are operated; tags are mutable, digests aren't Scope belongs to the test contract (aval.yaml); nothing is inferred or traced the test author knows what the test depends on, and a declared scope can be reviewed in a PR Fail closed: if input equivalence can't be proven, the test runs. A miss (exit 4) and a verification failure (exit 5) stay separate, and the latter is never downgraded a false hit costs more than a re-run, and a forged result is something someone needs to look at Trust levels (developer, runner, isolated) granted by the policy; no policy, no reuse how much a signed claim is worth depends on where it was produced, and that call belongs to the consumer Test identity (metadata.name) is not the execution fingerprint the same check gets many executions, and policy and reporting need to tell them apart Cacheability classes; non-deterministic is never reusable a matching fingerprint only means something if the result depends on the declared inputs One generic runner: an argv command, the exit code is the result it covers every language, framework and CI vendor

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• No registry, server or database of our own.
  • No runtime tracing or input inference in v0; "observed inputs" is future work, to check declared scope, not replace it.
  • Not a build system or a Bazel replacement.
  • Not a test framework: Aval records an exit code, not test cases.
  • No knowledge of Pacto or any other consumer; consumers use the stable formats.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Signal it isn't working Bazel or a remote cache is already enough target tests outside a hermetic build graph (integration, e2e, cross-environment) early users are mostly Bazel shops that want Aval for build actions Declaring scope costs more than it saves a small contract (globs, lockfiles, a toolchain map), debuggable with aval run --explain contracts drift from the code, or teams give up on wide-scope tests Inputs always change, so savings are small the docs say a "whole repo" scope is a bad fit a low hit rate in the example and in early adopters' pipelines Security policies reject developer signatures expected: CI requires runner or higher; developer stays personal the value does not hold with only runner and isolated signatures

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
# Milestone Status Done when 1 Fingerprint and contract implemented aval.yaml is validated with unknown fields rejected, and --fingerprint-only / --explain give a deterministic aval-fingerprint/v1 digest that fails closed on unprovable inputs 2 Push and verify against a registry, with signing implemented aval run --push signs and publishes; aval verify and aval run reuse a trusted result (exit 0), report a miss (exit 4) and a tampered or untrusted one (exit 5); the policy format is defined 3 End-to-end example in GitHub Actions in progress (CI quality gates) a public example where one run publishes, an unchanged run reuses, and a changed run misses, all visible in the logs 4 False-hit suite implemented (false-hit suite, known gaps) every known kind of relevant change is shown not to reuse a previous execution 5 Stable consumption contract in progress the formats, pkg/evidence and the verify report are versioned with only additive changes in v1, and an external consumer verifies with pkg/evidence alone 6 Contract composition for monorepos (Epic 10) in progress: scope.contracts binds other local contracts, transitively (guide) a test in a monorepo reruns when, and only when, the declared inputs of the parts it depends on change

A remote dependency (another repository, by OCI reference) is an idea, not built: its files are not available to fingerprint, so it would bind a published, verified result instead, which raises its own trust questions.

docs.title: How Aval works
docs.text:
Aval runs a test once, signs the result and stores it in your OCI registry. The next job with the same inputs checks that signature and skips the test.

flowchart LR
  run([aval run]) --> fp[fingerprint] --> look[look up] --> verify{trusted?}
  verify -- yes --> reuse([reuse]):::ok
  verify -- no --> exec[run the test] --> sign[sign] --> push([push]):::muted

docs.title: The steps
docs.text:
Step What happens Fingerprint hash aval.yaml and every input it declares into one sha256 Look up ask your registry for results under that fingerprint Verify the signature must come from a signer your policy trusts Reuse or run verified: the test is skipped. Anything else: it runs (Outcomes) Push with --push, sign the new result and push it

If Aval cannot prove reuse is safe, the test runs. See it run: Quickstart.

docs.title: What Aval does not do
docs.text:
• It does not guess inputs: a file the contract does not list is invisible to it.
  • It runs no server. Results live in an OCI registry you already have.

Details: the test contract, the trust model, the artifact format.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Hover a dotted word anywhere in the docs to see its short form.

Term Meaning More Attestation a signed statement: test X, with inputs that hash to fingerprint F, produced result R, stored in your OCI registry artifact format Cacheability how safe a test is to reuse: hermetic and controlled-environment yes, external-dependencies only if the policy allows it, non-deterministic never classes Contract aval.yaml: what the test is, how to run it, which inputs it reads the test contract Fingerprint one sha256 of every declared input: the contract (command included), files in scope, toolchain, env var values, resolved references. Same inputs, same fingerprint what goes in Mutable reference a tag or range that can point at other content later, such as postgres:16. In a hermetic or controlled-environment test it blocks reuse until you pin it or list it in scope.allowMutable Pin your dependencies Outcome the decision on a lookup: verified, miss, verification-failed or error. Only verified skips the test Outcomes Policy your YAML file listing trusted signers and their levels. No policy, no reuse Trust Scope the inputs the contract lists: source, dependencies (such as go.mod), resolve and contracts. Aval sees nothing else the test contract Signer who signed a result: a CI job (keyless, OIDC) or a key Trust Trust level how much the policy trusts a signer: developer, runner, isolated. Reuse needs at least minTrustLevel Trust

docs.title: Outcomes
docs.text:
Every lookup ends in one of four outcomes. Only verified skips the test.

flowchart LR
  start([look up]) --> decide{could Aval<br>decide?}
  decide -- no --> error([error<br>exit 1]):::warn
  decide -- yes --> found{result<br>found?}
  found -- no --> miss([miss<br>exit 4]):::muted
  found -- yes --> valid{verifies?}
  valid -- yes --> verified([verified<br>exit 0]):::ok
  valid -- no --> failed([verification-failed<br>exit 5]):::err

The exit codes in the diagram are those of aval verify. All of them:

Code aval run aval verify aval push 0 the test passed, or a verified passing result was reused a verified result exists (passing or failing) pushed 1 error (the test still runs when it can), or a false hit in --shadow error: registry, policy, trusted root or fingerprint error: signing, registry or a result that does not match the current inputs 2 bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml 3 the test failed, or a verified failing result was reused not used not used 4 not used: a miss runs the test miss: no result the policy can reuse not used 5 verification failed, after running the test: a security event verification failed: a security event not used 6 reserved, never returned reserved, never returned reserved, never returned

A miss (4) is routine. A verification failure (5) means someone published a result the policy does not trust; never hide it or retry it away.

docs.title: The four outcomes
docs.text: Outcome What it means aval run does verified a trusted result exists for these exact inputs reuses it: exit 0 for a pass, 3 for a failure miss nothing to reuse: the inputs changed, or nobody ran them yet runs the test error Aval could not decide, such as a registry it cannot reach runs the test verification-failed a result exists but does not verify runs the test, then exits 5

docs.title: A miss is routine
docs.text:
The normal case for a pull request: you changed an input, so there is nothing to reuse yet. Aval also reports a miss when:

  • there is no --policy (or, for aval run, no --registry, or --no-reuse)
  • the test is non-deterministic, or external-dependencies and not in the policy's allowedCacheability
  • the inputs hold a mutable reference you did not pin or list in scope.allowMutable
  • the only results are signed below minTrustLevel

docs.title: A verification failure is a security event
docs.text: A result under your fingerprint does not verify: a bad signature, a signer not in your policy, or a claim of other inputs. The cause is a wrong policy or an attacker. Aval runs the test, prints aval: SECURITY: ... and exits 5. Fail the job and investigate; never hide or retry it.

docs.title: In a script
docs.text:
Branch on the exit code of aval verify:

aval verify --registry "$REG" --policy policy.yaml
case $? in
  0) echo "a trusted result exists" ;;
  4) echo "miss: the test must run" ;;
  5) echo "SECURITY: a result failed verification" >&2; exit 1 ;;
  *) echo "error: the test must run" ;;
esac

Details: the JSON report in the artifact format.

docs.title: Trust
docs.text:
A signed result is reused only if your policy trusts the signer. The result cannot vouch for itself.

flowchart LR
  ci[CI job] --> r[signed result]
  dev[developer key] --> r
  r --> sig{valid<br>signature?}
  sig -- no --> fail([verification-failed<br>exit 5]):::err
  sig -- yes --> who{signer in<br>the policy?}
  who -- no --> fail
  who -- yes --> lvl{level high<br>enough?}
  lvl -- no --> miss([miss<br>exit 4]):::muted
  lvl -- yes --> ok([verified<br>reuse]):::ok

What each outcome means: Outcomes.

docs.title: Signers and levels
docs.text:
Signer Signs with Usual level CI job (keyless) a short-lived Sigstore certificate for its OIDC identity runner key a local ECDSA P-256 key file developer

Your policy sets the level. The level the result claims is ignored.

Level Name Constant Who Good for 0 unknown TrustUnknown level could not be established never accepted 1 developer TrustDeveloper a developer's local signature personal acceleration only: skip a test you already ran on your machine. Not full trust. 2 runner TrustRunner a CI runner with a verifiable workload identity (e.g. GitHub Actions OIDC) reuse in CI. CI should require at least this level. 3 isolated TrustIsolated an isolated execution with a verifiable attestation of the environment itself reuse where the runner host is not trusted either

docs.title: The policy
docs.text:
A policy is a YAML file in your repository. This one trusts the main workflow at runner level and Alice's key at developer level:

apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner           # developer | runner | isolated
# trustedRoot: sigstore/trusted_root.json  # keyless only; default: Sigstore public-good, fetched with TUF
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/acme/orders/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner
  - publicKey: keys/alice.pub   # PEM public key file
    trustLevel: developer
allowedCacheability: [external-dependencies]

With minTrustLevel: runner, a result Alice signed is a miss: the test runs. Without --policy, nothing is trusted and every test runs.

docs.title: What a signature proves
docs.text:
• Proves: who signed the result, and that nobody changed it since.
  • Does not prove: that the test ran honestly, or that inputs outside the contract were the same.

So only grant a level to signers you would trust to run the test yourself.

Details: the trust model (keyless verification, every policy field, threats).

docs.title: Depend on another part of the repo
docs.text:
Goal: in a monorepo, rerun the frontend tests when the backend's inputs change, without copying the backend's globs.

flowchart LR
  f[frontend/aval.yaml] -- scope.contracts --> b[backend/aval.yaml]
  b --> bs(["backend scope: api/**"])
  f --> fs(["frontend scope: src/**, test.sh"])
  bs -. change .-> miss([frontend misses and runs]):::err

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
The frontend names the backend's contract:

frontend/aval.yaml
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: frontend
runner:
  command: ["sh", "test.sh"]
scope:
  source: ["src/**", "test.sh"]
  contracts: ["../backend/aval.yaml"]
cacheability: hermetic
backend/aval.yaml
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: backend
runner:
  command: ["go", "test", "./..."]
scope:
  source: ["api/**"]
cacheability: hermetic

The frontend's fingerprint now includes the backend's fingerprint:

  • a change in the backend's scope makes the frontend miss and run;
  • a change outside it (a backend README) keeps the reuse;
  • if the backend names another contract, that one counts too.

aval run --explain shows the reference:

contract ../backend/aval.yaml backend sha256:<backend fingerprint>
depends on ../backend/aval.yaml (backend) sha256:<backend fingerprint>

docs.title: What to know
docs.text:
• Paths are relative to the contract and stay inside its git working tree. Only local files: no contract from another repository.
  • If Aval cannot read or fingerprint the referenced contract, the test runs.
  • A mutable reference in the backend blocks the frontend's reuse too. Only the backend's own scope.allowMutable can accept it.

Limits and errors: scope.contracts.

docs.title: A contract, or an API file?
docs.text:
Name the contract when the test runs the other part's code, like frontend end-to-end tests against the real backend.

When the test only uses the interface (a generated client, a mocked backend), list the API file (OpenAPI, .proto) in scope.dependencies instead. Only an interface change reruns the test. Globs cannot leave the contract's directory, so keep the file in the frontend's tree.

docs.title: Use GitHub Actions
docs.text:
Goal: a workflow on main that reuses a verified test result, or runs the test and publishes a signed one.

flowchart LR
  job([push to main]) --> run[aval run]
  run -- verified --> skip([test skipped]):::ok
  run -- anything else --> test[test runs] --> push[aval push] --> reg([GHCR]):::muted
  test -- "failed or exit 5" --> fail([step fails,<br>nothing pushed]):::err

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Copy these steps from Aval's own ci.yaml and set REPO, CONTRACT and POLICY. Install aval first with the installer.

The job needs these permissions:

    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
      id-token: write

The steps log in to GHCR, run the test or reuse the result, and publish a new result signed with the workflow's identity:

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          echo "$GH_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u "$GITHUB_ACTOR" --password-stdin
          echo "| step | outcome |" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          echo "|---|---|" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
      - name: Publish (runs and pushes unless a verified result exists)
        run: |
          aval run -f "$CONTRACT" --registry "$REPO" --policy "$POLICY" --report publish.json
          if [ "$(jq -r .outcome publish.json)" != "verified" ]; then
            # The Actions OIDC token for Fulcio, fetched after the test so a
            # slow test cannot outlive it. aval push reads SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN.
            SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN=$(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \
              "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=sigstore" | jq -r .value)
            export SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN
            aval push -f "$CONTRACT" --registry "$REPO"
          fi
          echo "| publish | \`$(jq -r .outcome publish.json)\` |" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

Trust only this workflow on main: see Write a trust policy.

Why the token is fetched after the test

The OIDC token is short-lived. Fetching it after the test means a slow test cannot outlive it. aval push reads it from $SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN; runner.command never sees it.

Pull requests

packages: write and id-token: write are write scopes, so this job runs only on push to main. A pull request job can still reuse: give it contents: read, run aval run with --registry and --policy, and leave out the push. GHCR packages that are public can be read without a login.

docs.title: Consume from Go
docs.text:
Goal: check an Aval result from your own Go program with pkg/evidence, and tell a miss from a security event.

flowchart LR
  fetch([envelope bytes,<br>fetched by digest]) --> check[Check]
  check -- nil bytes --> miss([ErrNotFound:<br>run the test]):::muted
  check -- ErrVerification --> alert([alert,<br>do not reuse]):::err
  check -- ok --> p([predicate]):::ok

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Add the module:

go get github.com/TrianaLab/aval@latest

This is Check from examples/evidence-consumer, a separate module that imports only pkg/evidence. CI builds and tests it:

// Check returns the verified predicate of a DSSE envelope fetched by digest.
// nil envBytes means the lookup found nothing: evidence.ErrNotFound, a miss.
// Every other failure wraps evidence.ErrVerification, a security event. The
// caller runs the test unless Check returns a passed predicate.
func Check(ctx context.Context, envBytes []byte, opts evidence.VerifyOptions) (*evidence.Predicate, error) {
    if envBytes == nil {
        return nil, evidence.ErrNotFound
    }
    var env evidence.Envelope
    if err := json.Unmarshal(envBytes, &env); err != nil {
        return nil, &evidence.VerificationError{Reason: "decoding envelope: " + err.Error()}
    }
    v, err := evidence.Verify(ctx, &env, opts)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return v.Predicate, nil
}

Branch on what it returns, with errors.Is:

Check returns Meaning Do a predicate with Result == evidence.ResultPassed a trusted pass for these inputs reuse it evidence.ErrNotFound nothing to reuse: a miss run the test evidence.ErrVerification a result that does not verify alert, run the test, do not reuse a predicate with another Result a trusted failure for these inputs treat the test as failed

docs.title: What you bring
docs.text:
• The envelope bytes. Fetch them by digest with ORAS or any registry client. The layout is in Artifact format.
  • A SignatureVerifier. pkg/evidence checks the policy, not the cryptography. The example brings an ed25519 one; a Sigstore one for consumers is planned for milestone 5.
  • The identities. Build them from your own policy. Trust never comes from the predicate.
Read an aval verify report instead

If you run aval verify --output json, read its report with evidence.Report. The example's Reuse function does this and fails closed on any verification-failed candidate.

docs.title: Measure reuse
docs.text:
Goal: find out how often Aval would reuse a result, and whether reuse would have been right, before you let it skip any test.

flowchart LR
  run([aval run --shadow]) --> v[verify] --> t[run the test anyway]
  t --> same{same result?}
  same -- yes --> ok([reuse would be correct]):::ok
  same -- no --> fh([FALSE HIT, exit 1]):::err

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Run in shadow mode and record every run:

aval run --shadow --record --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml
You see It means shadow: reuse of <ref> would have been correct safe to turn shadow off for this test aval: FALSE HIT: ... (exit 1) the contract misses an input: fix scope

docs.title: Record where you can write
docs.text:
--record publishes one run record per run, next to your results. To keep records apart, write them to a file and publish them with aval record to a registry of your own:

aval run --record-file record.json --repository acme/orders \
  --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml
aval record --record-file record.json --registry ghcr.io/acme/aval-stats

A test job without write access only writes the file; a job with write access, which runs no tests, runs aval record.

docs.title: Read the numbers
docs.text:
aval stats reads the records back and sums them per test: hits, misses by cause, verification failures, shadow false hits and time saved.

aval stats --registry ghcr.io/acme/aval-stats --since 7d

--by repository needs --repository <name> on aval run or aval record.

run records in ghcr.io/acme/aval-stats since 2026-10-31T12:30:00Z
orders-unit: 1 runs, 1 reused (hit rate 100.0%), test time 0s, saved 1m30s
  not reused: 0 no trusted result, 0 error, 0 verified but run (shadow)
  verification failures: 0, shadow false hits: 0
total: 1 runs, 1 reused (hit rate 100.0%), test time 0s, saved 1m30s
  not reused: 0 no trusted result, 0 error, 0 verified but run (shadow)
  verification failures: 0, shadow false hits: 0

--test limits it to one test, and -o json prints the stats report. aval stats writes nothing and never affects reuse.

Records are statistics, not evidence

Records are unsigned. aval run and aval verify never read them, so a forged record cannot cause reuse. Recording is best-effort: a record that cannot be published prints aval: warning: run record not published and never changes the exit code.

What the fields mean

reused is true when the test did not run. savedDurationMs is how long the reused run took when it was recorded. With --shadow, reused is always false. Every field is in Artifact format: run records.

{
  "version": "aval.trianalab.io/run-record/v1",
  "testId": "orders-integration",
  "fingerprint": "sha256:3f9a7c2e1b4d5f60718293a4b5c6d7e8f9012a3b4c5d6e7f8091a2b3c4d5e6f7",
  "outcome": "verified",
  "reused": true,
  "result": "passed",
  "verifiedResult": "passed",
  "testDurationMs": 0,
  "savedDurationMs": 1184000,
  "avalVersion": "0.3.0",
  "recordedAt": "2026-11-06T09:00:00Z",
  "ciRunUrl": "https://ci.example.com/acme/orders/runs/42",
  "repository": "acme/orders"
}

docs.title: Sign results
docs.text:
Goal: sign a test result so that others can check who published it.

flowchart LR
  run([aval run]) --> result[.aval/result.json] --> push[aval push]
  push -- key file --> keyed([key-based]):::muted
  push -- OIDC token --> keyless([keyless]):::ok

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
KeyKeyless

Make a P-256 key and a policy that trusts it:

openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key
openssl pkey -in aval.key -pubout -out aval.pub
cat > policy.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: developer
identities:
  - publicKey: aval.pub
    trustLevel: developer
EOF

Run the test, then sign and push the result:

aval run --push --key aval.key --registry localhost:5001/demo/hello-aval

Put an OIDC token in $SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN and leave out --key:

export SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN="<OIDC token for audience sigstore>"
aval run --push --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval

On GitHub Actions the job gets the token itself; see Use GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Which one
docs.text:
Key Keyless Who signs whoever holds the key file a CI job or a person, proven by an OIDC token Policy entry publicKey: aval.pub issuer and subjectRegexp Typical trust level developer runner Needs network to verify no yes, unless the policy pins trustedRoot Which keys work

An unencrypted ECDSA P-256 key in PEM (PKCS#8 or SEC1). Cosign keys are encrypted and do not work. Make one with openssl genpkey -algorithm EC -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -out aval.key.

Sign later with aval push

aval run records the result in .aval/result.json. aval push signs and publishes it later, with the same --key or token. It refuses a result whose inputs no longer match the contract:

aval run --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml
aval push --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval

Goal: go from an exit code or an error message to its cause and its fix.

flowchart LR

  code -- 1 --> e([Errors]):::warn

docs.title: Start with the exit code
docs.text:
aval verify --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml; echo "exit $?"
Code aval run aval verify aval push 0 the test passed, or a verified passing result was reused a verified result exists (passing or failing) pushed 1 error (the test still runs when it can), or a false hit in --shadow error: registry, policy, trusted root or fingerprint error: signing, registry or a result that does not match the current inputs 2 bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml bad flags or invalid aval.yaml 3 the test failed, or a verified failing result was reused not used not used 4 not used: a miss runs the test miss: no result the policy can reuse not used 5 verification failed, after running the test: a security event verification failed: a security event not used 6 reserved, never returned reserved, never returned reserved, never returned

A miss (4) is routine. A verification failure (5) means someone published a result the policy does not trust; never hide it or retry it away.

docs.title: Write a trust policy
docs.text:
Goal: a policy.yaml that says whose results you reuse, and nobody else's.

flowchart LR
  p([policy.yaml]) --> id["identities:<br>issuer + subjectRegexp,<br>or publicKey"] --> tl[trustLevel] --> min{"≥ minTrustLevel?"}
  min -- yes --> ok([reuse]):::ok
  min -- no --> m([miss]):::muted

The full decision, signature included: Trust.

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
Trust one GitHub Actions workflow on main. This is the policy of the example-go-compose job in Aval's CI:

# Trust policy for the GitHub Actions demo (the example-go-compose job in
# .github/workflows/ci.yaml): reuse only results signed keyless by that
# workflow on main. Anything else that sits under the fingerprint, such as a
# result signed with some key, is a verification failure (exit 5).
apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Policy
minTrustLevel: runner
identities:
  - issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
    subjectRegexp: https://github\.com/TrianaLab/aval/\.github/workflows/ci\.yaml@refs/heads/main
    trustLevel: runner

For a key, see Sign results. Use it with --policy:

aval verify --registry ghcr.io/acme/orders-aval --policy policy.yaml

docs.title: The fields
docs.text: Field Meaning identities the signers you accept: each is an OIDC issuer plus a subjectRegexp matched against the whole certificate subject, or a publicKey PEM file. At least one. trustLevel the level an identity gets: developer, runner or isolated. minTrustLevel the lowest level a result needs to be reused. allowedCacheability classes reused besides hermetic and controlled-environment; only external-dependencies has an effect, and non-deterministic is rejected. trustedRoot a pinned Sigstore trusted root for keyless signatures; without it, the public-good root is fetched.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Anchor the subject to one workflow file and one branch. A pull request branch can run any code, so do not trust it at runner level.
  • Give developer keys developer; keep minTrustLevel: runner in CI so CI never reuses laptop results.
How the subject is matched

subjectRegexp must match the whole subject, as if it started with ^ and ended with $. Escape dots: github\.com. For GitHub Actions the subject is https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/<workflow path>@<ref>.

Keyless checks and the network

A keyless policy fetches the Sigstore trusted root on first use and caches it under $HOME/.sigstore. Offline, that candidate is an error and the test runs. Pin the root with trustedRoot to avoid this; see the trust model.

docs.text:
Goal: an aval.yaml that lists every input of your test, so a result is reused only when none of them changed.

flowchart LR
  c([aval.yaml]) --> s[scope: files the test reads] --> fp[fingerprint]
  c --> k[cacheability: how safe reuse is] --> d{reusable?}

docs.title: The example
docs.text:
This contract runs a Go integration test against Redis from Docker Compose. It is examples/go-compose/aval.yaml, which CI runs:

apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: counter-integration
runner:
  command: ["sh", "-c", "docker compose up -d --wait && REDIS_ADDR=localhost:16379 go test -tags=integration -count=1 ./...; rc=$?; docker compose down; exit $rc"]
scope:
  source: ["**/*.go", "compose.yaml"]
  dependencies: [go.mod]
environment:
  toolchain: {go: "1.25"}
cacheability: controlled-environment

Put it next to your test and check what it hashes:

aval run --explain --fingerprint-only

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1. Name the test. metadata.name says what is checked. It stays the same when the inputs change.
  2. Say how to run it. runner.command is an argv list. Aval does not use a shell unless you call one, like the example does.
  3. List the inputs. scope.source lists the files the test reads. scope.dependencies lists dependency manifests and lockfiles (go.mod, go.sum). Globs are relative to the contract's directory; ** matches any number of directories.
  4. Pick a cacheability class. It tells Aval and the policy how safe reuse is. Tags, ranges and branches block reuse for hermetic and controlled-environment: see Pin your dependencies.
Class Use it when Reused hermetic the test reads only the declared files yes controlled-environment it uses services you pin, such as a Compose image by digest yes external-dependencies it calls something you do not control only if the policy allows it non-deterministic the same inputs can give a different result never

docs.title: Resolve references
docs.text:
The fingerprint hashes the text of your files. postgres:16 is hashed as the words postgres:16, not as the image behind them. Pinning fixes that by writing the immutable id into a file: a digest, a lockfile, a commit. When you cannot or do not want to pin, declare the reference in scope.resolve: Aval looks up what the name points to every time it fingerprints, and hashes that id.

apiVersion: aval.trianalab.io/v1
kind: Test
metadata:
  name: orders-integration
runner:
  command: ["docker", "compose", "run", "--rm", "tests"]
scope:
  source: ["**/*.go", "compose.yaml"]
  resolve:
    - image: postgres:16
    - npm: prettier@^3
    - git: https://github.com/acme/fixtures@main
cacheability: controlled-environment

When someone repushes postgres:16, publishes any new prettier release or moves main, the id changes, the fingerprint changes, and Aval runs the test instead of reusing an old result.

docs.title: Exact or floating
docs.text:
For npm, PyPI, crates, gems and Maven, an exact version binds that release. Anything else (a range, latest, a tag) binds the whole release list, so any new release runs the test again. Aval never picks a version from a range.

Kind Exact Floating hashes npm x.y.z[-pre] every version's dist.integrity and deprecation, every dist-tag pypi one == without * every file's sha256 and yanked flag crate =x.y.z every index entry's checksum and yanked flag gem a plain version every version and platform checksum maven a plain version every listed version's POM and checksums (100 versions at most) go vX.Y.Z (a branch or commit resolves to a version) the version list, plus @latest and its h1: hash, for latest, a prefix, a comparison or +incompatible image the tag's manifest digest git a full commit the commit a branch or tag points to url the bytes

A publish, a yank or a moved tag changes the id: the test runs more often, never on stale inputs. When in doubt, a spec is floating. A spec the tool installs from elsewhere (npm:x, github:, file:, ./dir) or a name outside the ecosystem's rules fails: use git or url, or pin. Each page lists the rules.

docs.title: Pin or resolve?
docs.text:
Pin (digest, lockfile, commit) Resolve (scope.resolve) Works offline; the fingerprint needs no network. Needs the registry every time Aval fingerprints. You update the pin by hand or with a bot. You follow a tag or a branch on purpose; a range follows every release. What you run is what you hashed. The id is read when Aval fingerprints; a push between that and your test's own download is not seen.

Prefer pinning. Use scope.resolve for references you mean to follow: a nightly base image, a tool at latest, a fixtures branch.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The manifest gets one line per reference, after the env lines: resolve <kind> <reference> <version> <id>, where <version> is floating for a reference that names no exact version. aval run --explain shows them, and prints on stderr how long each lookup took, including those of the contracts in scope.contracts.
  • The list is part of the contract hash; its order and duplicates do not matter. Contracts without scope.resolve never touch the network.
  • scope.resolve binds the artifact you name, not its dependencies. npm, pip, cargo install without --locked and gem install still pick transitive versions when they install. Pin those with a lockfile.
  • No cache: every fingerprint asks the registry again.

docs.title: scope.resolve and the scanner
docs.text: scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

docs.title: When resolution fails
docs.text: A reference that cannot be resolved (network, credentials, an exact version that is not published, a listed version without a checksum, a download over 256 MiB, the 2-minute deadline) fails the fingerprint. Nothing is looked up, the test runs, and the reason names the reference: fingerprint: resolve npm left@9.9.9: version 9.9.9 is not published. aval verify exits 1; aval run --push runs the test and publishes nothing.

docs.title: Registries and credentials
docs.text:
Kind Registry (default) Credentials image the host in the reference (Docker Hub) Docker config (docker login) npm $npm_config_registry (registry.npmjs.org) //host/:_authToken= in ~/.npmrc, else ~/.netrc pypi $AVAL_PYPI_URL (pypi.org, JSON API) ~/.netrc go first proxy in $GOPROXY (proxy.golang.org) ~/.netrc maven $AVAL_MAVEN_URL (repo.maven.apache.org/maven2) ~/.netrc crate $AVAL_CRATES_INDEX (index.crates.io, sparse) ~/.netrc gem $AVAL_RUBYGEMS_URL (rubygems.org) ~/.netrc git the URL in the reference git's own (credential helpers, SSH keys) url the URL in the reference ~/.netrc
  • Only machine entries of ~/.netrc (or $NETRC) are used, never default, and only over https or to a loopback host (also after a redirect). $npm_config_userconfig (any letter case) points npm's file elsewhere. Credentials go in headers, never in the manifest, a URL or an error; a user, password or path in a registry variable is masked in errors and refused over plain http to a host that is not loopback.
  • A reference with credentials is rejected without echoing it: a password in any URL, a user in an http(s) or scheme-less //user@host URL (an ssh://git@host user is fine), an @ in the authority of a URL that does not parse, or a query parameter named token, private_token, access_token, key, apikey, api_key, sig, signature, X-Amz-Signature, X-Goog-Signature, auth, password, secret, credential, security_token, x_amz_security_token, client_secret, session or sessionid (any case, - read as _, a trailing [] ignored).
  • The registry address is not hashed: the same content on a mirror resolves to the same id. Requests carry the User-Agent aval/<version> (+https://github.com/TrianaLab/aval).

The resolved id vouches for the registry in the table, not for the one the tool installs from. Where the tool's own setting points elsewhere, resolution fails:

Kind Fails when npm ~/.npmrc has a @scope:registry or registry line, or an npm_config_@scope:registry variable is set, that differs from Aval's registry; two spellings of an npm_config_* variable differ; a ~/.npmrc line cannot be read go $GOPROXY starts with direct or off; $GOPRIVATE or $GONOPROXY matches; GOSUMDB=off, $GONOSUMDB, $GOINSECURE or -insecure in $GOFLAGS pypi $PIP_INDEX_URL or $PIP_PYPI_URL names another index; $PIP_EXTRA_INDEX_URL or $PIP_FIND_LINKS is set; $PIP_NO_INDEX is true (any spelling pip reads); two spellings of one PIP_* variable (the option in any case, - equal to _, an optional leading --; on Windows PIP_ in any case) differ maven <latest> or <release> is a SNAPSHOT or not listed

Not read: pip.conf, a project .npmrc, go env -w settings, Cargo's config.toml, Maven's settings.xml, .gemrc. If one of them points the tool to another registry, set the Aval variable to the same registry.

docs.title: Rust crates
docs.text:
crate: <name>@=<version> hashes the .crate checksum of that version from the crates.io index.

For npm, PyPI, crates, gems and Maven, an exact version binds that release. Anything else (a range, latest, a tag) binds the whole release list, so any new release runs the test again. Aval never picks a version from a range.

scope:
  resolve:
    - crate: cargo-nextest@=0.9.81   # exact
    - crate: serde@1                 # floating (Cargo reads it as ^1)
    - crate: tokio                   # floating
  • Exact means Cargo's =x.y.z; a bare 1.2.3 means ^1.2.3, so it is floating. A yanked version is not resolved: Cargo does not pick it either.
  • The name is a crates.io name (a letter, then up to 63 letters, digits, _ or -). A spec with :, / or #, or starting with . or ~/, fails: use git or url, or pin.
  • Floating: every index entry with its checksum and yanked flag.
  • Index $AVAL_CRATES_INDEX (sparse protocol); credentials from ~/.netrc.

Pin instead for your crate's dependencies: commit Cargo.lock and add it to scope.dependencies. Resolve is for cargo install tool in runner.command. Only the crate is bound: without --locked, cargo install picks new versions of its dependencies.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

docs.title: Ruby gems
docs.text:
gem: <name>@<version> hashes the checksums of all platform gems of that version.

For npm, PyPI, crates, gems and Maven, an exact version binds that release. Anything else (a range, latest, a tag) binds the whole release list, so any new release runs the test again. Aval never picks a version from a range.

scope:
  resolve:
    - gem: rubocop@1.66.1   # exact
    - gem: rails@~>7.1      # floating
    - gem: bundler          # floating
  • Exact means a plain version (7.1.3, 7.2.0.beta1) with no operator. It binds every number RubyGems holds equal to it (7.1.3.0 too).
  • The name is a RubyGems name (a letter or digit, then letters, digits, ., _ or -). A spec with :, / or #, starting with . or ~/, or a name ending in .gem fails: use git or url, or pin.
  • gem install also reads a matching <name>-<version>.gem file in the current directory, which Aval does not see: run it where no such file lies.
  • Floating: every version, platform and checksum.
  • Registry $AVAL_RUBYGEMS_URL; credentials from ~/.netrc.

Pin instead for your application's gems: commit Gemfile.lock and add it to scope.dependencies. Resolve is for gem install tool in runner.command. Only the gem is bound, not the dependencies gem install picks.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

docs.title: Git references
docs.text:
git: <url>@<ref> asks the remote, with git ls-remote, which commit a branch or tag points to, and hashes the commit id.

scope:
  resolve:
    - git: https://github.com/acme/fixtures@main
    - git: https://github.com/acme/fixtures@v1.4.0   # an annotated tag: its commit
    - git: ssh://git@github.com/acme/private@refs/heads/release
  • The ref is a branch, a tag, HEAD or a full ref name. A name that is both a branch and a tag fails: write refs/heads/<name> or refs/tags/<name>. A full commit id resolves to itself, unless a branch or tag has that exact name, which fails.
  • URLs: https, http, ssh, git or file, with a scheme (ssh://git@host/repo, not git@host:repo).
  • Needs git on the PATH. Credentials come from git itself: credential helpers, SSH keys. Git never prompts.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

The entry hashes the commit, so a moved branch changes the fingerprint.

Pin instead with a commit: git clone URL && git -C dir checkout <40-hex>, or a submodule. Resolve is for a branch you mean to follow, such as shared test fixtures.

docs.title: Go modules
docs.text:
go: <module>@<query> hashes the module zip the way go.sum does (h1:). What a query binds depends on its form, as the go command reads it:

Query Binds vX.Y.Z, optional -pre (pseudo-versions too) that version's zip (exact) a branch, a commit or another non-semver query (main, 4f3c2a1) the zip of the version the proxy resolves it to, usually a pseudo-version; the manifest line names it latest (or no query), a prefix (v1.2), a comparison (<v1.3.0), +incompatible the proxy's version list, its @latest and that version's h1: hash (floating) 
scope:
  resolve:
    - go: golang.org/x/tools@v0.26.0   # exact: binds v0.26.0
    - go: github.com/acme/lib@main     # a branch: binds its current commit
    - go: golang.org/x/net@latest      # floating: binds the version list
  • For a floating query, other versions are bound by name: the checksum database keeps every version the go command accepts fixed.
  • The module path must pass golang.org/x/mod's module.CheckPath, and names the module, not a package inside it.
  • Proxy: the first entry of $GOPROXY (https://proxy.golang.org); credentials from ~/.netrc.
  • Fails when the go command would bypass the proxy or the checksum database: $GOPROXY starting with direct or off, $GOPRIVATE or $GONOPROXY matching, GOSUMDB=off, $GONOSUMDB or $GOINSECURE matching, or -insecure in $GOFLAGS. go env -w settings are not read. Aval never clones: pin the module or use git.

Pin instead for your module's dependencies: commit go.sum and add it to scope.dependencies. Resolve is for go install tool@v1.2.3 in runner.command.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

docs.title: Container images
docs.text:
image: <name>:<tag> resolves the tag to the digest of its manifest. For a multi-arch image that is the digest of the index, so a new build for any platform changes it.

scope:
  source: ["compose.yaml", "**/*.go"]
  resolve:
    - image: postgres:16                     # Docker Hub
    - image: ghcr.io/acme/orders-db:nightly  # any OCI registry
  • A name without a host is a Docker Hub name: postgres:16 is docker.io/library/postgres:16, and so are docker.io/postgres:16 and index.docker.io/postgres:16. No tag means latest.
  • The digest Aval reads is the registry's, not the runner's. Compose without pull_policy: always, or Kubernetes with IfNotPresent, can run a copy pulled earlier: pull before the test, or pin by digest.
  • Also covers what the scanner cannot see, such as Helm values that split repository and tag: declare the image those values make.
  • Credentials come from docker login ($DOCKER_CONFIG). A loopback registry (localhost:5000) is reached over plain HTTP.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

Pin instead when you want what you run to be exactly what you hashed: image: postgres:16@sha256:<digest> in the file. Find the digest with crane digest postgres:16.

docs.title: Maven artifacts
docs.text:
maven: <group>:<artifact>:<version> hashes the POM of that version together with the checksums the repository publishes for its artifacts (.sha256, else .sha1).

For npm, PyPI, crates, gems and Maven, an exact version binds that release. Anything else (a range, latest, a tag) binds the whole release list, so any new release runs the test again. Aval never picks a version from a range.

scope:
  resolve:
    - maven: org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.4         # exact
    - maven: org.junit:junit-bom:5.+                  # floating
    - maven: org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:RELEASE # floating
  • Group and artifact ids: a letter, digit or _, then letters, digits, _, . or -, with no ...
  • Exact means a plain version: no +, [, ( or ,, and not LATEST, RELEASE or latest.*.
  • Floating: the <versioning> block of maven-metadata.xml and each listed version's POM and checksums. No versions, more than 100 (popular artifacts such as guava list more than 200), or a <latest>/<release> that is a SNAPSHOT or not listed fails: use an exact version.
  • A SNAPSHOT version, in any case, fails, and so does a floating list that holds one: a snapshot is redeployed under the same name.
Packaging Bound jar (default), bundle, maven-plugin, ejb POM and .jar checksum (required) war, ear, rar, aar POM, that file's checksum, and the .jar checksum if present pom (a BOM or parent) POM, and the .jar checksum if present

A missing checksum, a checksum file that holds none (a proxy's error page) or another packaging fails. Aval never downloads the jar. Not covered:

  • classifier artifacts (-sources, -linux-x86_64)
  • Gradle module metadata (.module), from which Gradle can pick another file
  • a jar overwritten on a private repository without redeploying its checksum
  • a repository that publishes only .sha1: the id rests on SHA-1

Repository $AVAL_MAVEN_URL; credentials from ~/.netrc.

Pin instead in pom.xml or build.gradle with exact versions; Gradle can also lock dependencies (gradle.lockfile).

docs.title: npm packages
docs.text:
npm: <name>@<version> hashes the dist.integrity of that version.

For npm, PyPI, crates, gems and Maven, an exact version binds that release. Anything else (a range, latest, a tag) binds the whole release list, so any new release runs the test again. Aval never picks a version from a range.

scope:
  resolve:
    - npm: prettier@3.3.3      # exact: binds 3.3.3
    - npm: typescript@latest   # floating: binds every release and tag
    - npm: "@types/node@22.x"  # floating
  • Exact means x.y.z, with an optional -pre and no operator. A name without a version means latest. A spec with +build is never found (the registry strips it) and fails.
  • Fails for any spec npm installs from elsewhere: an alias (npm:other), github:, org/repo, git+https:, a tarball URL, file: or a path (any spec with :, /, # or \, starting with . or ~/, or ending in .tgz, .tar.gz or .tar). Use git or url, or pin.
  • The name follows npm's legacy rules, which npm still installs (JSONStream): at most 214 characters, an optional lowercase @scope/, then [A-Za-z0-9-~][A-Za-z0-9-._~]*. A name ending in .tgz, .tar.gz or .tar fails: npm reads it as a local file.
  • Floating: every version with its dist.integrity and deprecation, and every dist-tag. A publish, an unpublish, a deprecation or a moved tag changes the id.
  • Registry $npm_config_registry; token from the //host/:_authToken= line of ~/.npmrc (or $npm_config_userconfig), ${VAR} expanded. As in npm, npm_config_* variables are read in any letter case, with _ equal to - after the first character. A project .npmrc and the global npmrc are not read.
  • ~/.npmrc is read as npm reads it (ini: quotes removed, ; and # comments, keys under a [section] ignored). A line Aval cannot read as key=value fails the fingerprint, and no token is sent. Settings that point the package at another registry fail too (details).

Pin instead for your project's own dependencies: commit package-lock.json (or yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, bun.lock) and add it to scope.dependencies. Resolve is for a tool the test installs on its own, such as npx prettier@3.3.3. Only the package is bound, not the dependencies npm picks for it.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

docs.title: Python packages (PyPI)
docs.text:
pypi: <name>==<version> hashes the sha256 of every file of that release (sdist and wheels).

For npm, PyPI, crates, gems and Maven, an exact version binds that release. Anything else (a range, latest, a tag) binds the whole release list, so any new release runs the test again. Aval never picks a version from a range.

scope:
  resolve:
    - pypi: ruff==0.6.9        # exact: binds 0.6.9
    - pypi: requests==2.32.*   # floating: binds every release
    - pypi: pytest             # floating
  • Exact means one == clause with no *. Extras (requests[socks]) are ignored; environment markers are not supported.
  • ==X binds every release pip would match for it, including local labels (X+cu121) and zero-padded forms (X.0); ==X+label binds only that label. A wheel added to the release later changes the id. Other spellings of a pre-release (1.0c1 for 1.0rc1) are not grouped.
  • Floating: every file of every release, with its sha256 and yanked flag.
  • The name must be a PEP 508 name, with optional [extra,...]. A path, a URL, a marker or an archive file name (.whl, .tar.gz, .zip, ...) fails: pip would install it from disk or elsewhere. Use url.
  • Registry $AVAL_PYPI_URL (an index with the PyPI JSON API at /pypi/<name>/json); credentials from ~/.netrc. PIP_* variables that point pip elsewhere fail (details); pip.conf and uv settings are not read.

Pin instead for your requirements: pip-compile --generate-hashes or uv pip compile --generate-hashes, commit the file, and add it to the scope. Resolve is for a tool the test installs on its own, such as pip install ruff==0.6.9. Only the package is bound, not the dependencies pip picks for it.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

docs.title: Downloaded files
docs.text:
url: <url> downloads the file and hashes its bytes (sha256), up to 256 MiB.

scope:
  resolve:
    - url: https://github.com/acme/tool/releases/latest/download/tool-linux-amd64.tar.gz
    - url: https://example.com/install.sh
  • Also covers what the scanner does not detect: a curl -o tool URL or curl URL | tar x of a URL without a version. The same bytes under another URL give the same id.
  • https or http only. Credentials: ~/.netrc. A presigned URL is rejected (why).
  • Aval downloads the file every time it fingerprints, and the test downloads it again: a change between the two is not seen.

scope.resolve never clears a scanner finding: a move changes the fingerprint, but the reference still blocks reuse. Pin it in place, or accept it with scope.allowMutable.

Pin instead with a versioned URL and a checksum the test checks (sha256sum -c), or vendor the file into the scope.
